questions.prompt: On a 64-bit platform (8-byte pointers), what are the sizes of p1 (empty functor deleter) and p2 (function pointer deleter)?
options: Both p1 and p2 are 8 bytes
p1 is 8 bytes and p2 is 16 bytes
p1 is 16 bytes and p2 is 8 bytes
Both p1 and p2 are 16 bytes
questions.explanation: std::unique_ptr compresses an empty stateless functor deleter (like EmptyDeleter or std::default_delete) to zero extra bytes via empty-base optimization or [[no_unique_address]], so p1 stays 8 bytes. A function pointer void(*)(int*) carries runtime address state stored inside p2, doubling its size to 16 bytes.

questions.prompt: Two threads share access to an object observed through std::weak_ptr<Session> wp. What is the correct way to safely use the Session if it is still alive?
options: Call if (auto sp = wp.lock()) { sp->ping(); }
Call if (!wp.expired()) { wp.lock()->ping(); }
Cast wp with std::static_pointer_cast<Session>
Read wp.use_count() > 0 before calling wp.lock()
questions.explanation: Checking expired() or use_count() before locking creates a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race: another thread can destroy the final shared_ptr in between, causing wp.lock() to return null. Calling wp.lock() directly atomically checks and increments the strong reference count.

questions.prompt: A BigBuffer object is created via std::make_shared<BigBuffer>(), a std::weak_ptr<BigBuffer> observer is saved, and all std::shared_ptr handles are then destroyed while observer stays alive. What happens to BigBuffer's destructor and its heap memory?
options: Neither ~BigBuffer() runs nor is any memory freed until observer is destroyed
Both ~BigBuffer() runs and the entire heap allocation is freed immediately on sp.reset()
~BigBuffer() runs immediately on sp.reset(), but the underlying memory block stays allocated until observer expires
observer.lock() reconstructs BigBuffer on demand from the control block
questions.explanation: std::make_shared allocates the control block and BigBuffer in a single contiguous heap allocation. When the strong count hits zero, ~BigBuffer() is invoked immediately, yet the combined memory chunk cannot be passed to deallocate until weak_count also reaches zero.

questions.prompt: In the snippet below, src allocates from a stack monotonic_buffer_resource, whereas dst uses std::pmr::get_default_resource(). What happens during dst = std::move(src);?
options: dst steals src's buffer pointer in O(1) time and adopts arena as its allocator
Compilation fails because pmr::vector objects with different resources have incompatible types
Undefined behavior because arena and the default resource compare unequal
dst retains the default memory resource and moves/copies the elements into newly allocated storage because polymorphic_allocator's POCMA is false_type
questions.explanation: std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator defines propagate_on_container_move_assignment as std::false_type. Because dst.get_allocator() != src.get_allocator(), move assignment cannot transfer ownership of src's arena buffer and instead moves elements individually into memory allocated by dst's resource.

questions.prompt: Base has a non-virtual destructor and Derived publicly inherits from Base. Compare destroying sp (std::shared_ptr<Base>) vs destroying up (std::unique_ptr<Base>) when both were initialized from new Derived.
options: Both invoke undefined behavior when destroyed because Base lacks a virtual destructor
sp cleanly invokes ~Derived() via its control block's type-erased deleter, whereas up invokes undefined behavior (delete on Base* with non-virtual destructor)
up cleanly invokes ~Derived() via default_delete, whereas sp leaks s
Both safely invoke ~Derived() in C++20 and later
questions.explanation: std::shared_ptr<Base>(new Derived) captures the static type Derived* inside its control block's type-erased deleter at construction time, so teardown deletes the complete Derived object safely. By contrast, std::unique_ptr<Base> stores only std::default_delete<Base>, calling delete static_cast<Base*>(p), which is undefined behavior under [expr.delete] when ~Base() is non-virtual.

questions.prompt: A class Node publicly inherits from std::enable_shared_from_this<Node>. In C++17 and later, what happens if Node::Node() calls shared_from_this() inside its constructor body?
options: Returns a valid std::shared_ptr<Node> sharing the incoming make_shared control block
Silent undefined behavior with a null control block
Throws std::bad_weak_ptr because weak_this is not initialized until after Node construction finishes
Fails to compile unless Node is created via std::shared_ptr<Node>(new Node)
questions.explanation: The std::shared_ptr constructor populates enable_shared_from_this's internal weak_this member only after the managed Node object has finished constructing. Under C++17+ [util.smartptr.enab], shared_from_this() is specified as return shared_ptr<T>(weak_this), which throws std::bad_weak_ptr when weak_this is empty.
